review:
TLDR - Overall the game was good! I bought it on-sale ($3,99), and it was worth it.  I wouldn't pay the current $14.99 for it though, wait for a sale.

What I liked:
1. The story
2. The music
3. The puzzles were good, but probably could have been a little harder
4. The static camera angles (like Resident Evil)
5. Cinematic and interactive cut-scenes
6. The TV-series style episodes.  Before each episode it gives you a "previously on..." and also a "next on..." recap.  It made you feel like you're watching a TV show.

What I didn't like:
1. You had to do things in the order the game wants you to do them.  For example, I know I had to pick up a screwdriver to open a fuse box, but I couldn't pick it up until I interacted with the fuse box first and the game told me I needed the screwdriver.

2. It was too easy to find items.  Whenever the game requested you needed something, everything needed was in the same room.

3. Unnecessary "back" click you have to do after every interaction.

pros

+ unoriginal but engaging science fiction and conspiracy story in the post-apocalyptic world. there are some similarities with Soma.
+ well made cinematics
+ speaking and action choices can make affect your story progress and characters fate
+ good quality and polished graphics and character models
+ decent voice acting
+ mostly easy puzzles (if you don't want to challenge)
+ there are many characters that are becoming more and more interesting
+ nice background musics
+ there are steam achievements and cards
+ there is auto save

cons

- some frustrating puzzles towards to end. i wished skip option for them.
- the controls and automatic camera angles are frustrating at times.
- a few pixel huntings
- there are some slow paced and tedious parts. story little bit drags out and it could have been better paced.

Overall, this is an well made and polished interactive movie style adventure game. it's very similar to Telltale style games such as The Walking Dead.

The Descendant tries really hard. Somebody obviously put some thought into how the game would look, a style reminiscent of Telltale adventures. Decent taste in influences buoyed my hope... the vaults of Fallout decorated with the computers and cryogenic pods of the Alien franchise. Tragically, that kindred spirit wears thin within the first ten minutes. All components for a successful game are present, but they're sewn together with dental floss. The click-to-walk controls are endlessly frustrating; coupled with piss-poor fixed camera angles, the clunky maneuvers make you wonder if your character has been skipping meds. Occasionally you'll get to button mash while cranking valves or opening doors or something equally boring. These trifles are trumped by poor dialogue, amateurish voice acting, and tediously linear gameplay. I'd like to believe the story of The Descendant is worth telling, but it certainly isn't worth playing.

I liked the game but some things are not done well.

First of all, mouse-clicking movements are atrocious, meaning that is very difficult to choose where you want to go and the game always thinks otherwise.. At a given point you also get a map with a clickable icon on screen to reach some destinations in game which are not super easy to: well, clicking on the map icon also moves your character, so you lose perspective on where you were and where you are now.

Puzzles? They are easy in the first couple episode and get harder later on but it's because some are presented in a very wrong way that understanding what they want you to do is quite difficult.

Graphically speaking I found it odd that game is running at only 30FPS, even if this game genre doesn't require more of that.. (cutscenes are not capped instead and run at full frames/s). I liked the artwork tho, especially where there are close-ups or scenery to watch at.

Game language is English only but it's got subs (Italian, French, German and Spanish) and it's translated quite well, can't complain.

100% Achievements requires multiple playthroughs (choices matter)..

Overall a good experience, would recommend for some casual playing between your favorite games. It also goes up to 90% OFF when on sale.

It is the end of the world where only a few selected ones have been chosen to survive in Ark bunkers around USA. There are the special ones, called the "Descendants". And then, there are those at duty, called the "Janitors", who make sure the Arks run smoothly to keep the Descendants alive and safe.

"The Descendant" is a story about Ark-01 and you play the game from the perspective of these few characters:

1. Donald Freeman, a Janitor from Ark-42, who at the start of the story, arrived at Ark-01 with Randolph Jefferson, a former U.S. Senator before the bombs dropped. Their mission is to find out why the Descendants of Ark-01 have still not woken up from their cryo tanks.

2. Mia Howard, who was assigned to be one of the Janitors of Ark-01.

3. Silas, the first Janitor of Ark-01, who was expecting 11 more Janitors to help him with Ark-01, but only got Mia. (funny part is that he was expecting 11 more, but there were only 2 cryo tanks in the Janitors' quarters)

"The Descendant" is like a TellTale game where there are conversational choices for you to pick, with some puzzles here and there for you to solve in order for the story to progress. You should be able to complete the game in about 5 hours, but to get 100% Achievements, you will have to replay a few episodes/chapters. In my opinion, the choices you pick in this game do not matter much, [spoiler]except for the very last choice, which will affect how the ending will go[/spoiler].

There were a few bugs and glitches that I've experienced, which forced me to shut the game down and restart from the closest save point, but other than that, the game went on quite smoothly.

Overall, I enjoyed it, both the story and gameplay, and would recommend it! I hope the developers will make more games like this, as I'll be sure to support it!

Played Episode One.

The Descendant goes for the episodic Telltale mold, but fails to understand what made those games good. Instead of focusing on interesting characters, their personal relations and choices, we get cardboard cutout protagonists who don't have enough of a personality to even be called stereotypes.

It's the post-apocalypse again. And as established by post-apocalyptic rules, there's also a cryogenic vault. We get to follow two separate ventures into said vault; One maintenance crew shortly after and during the ICBM's hitting their targets, and one search & rescue crew hundreds of years later, wading through the derelict bunker.

I'm going to call these people the janitor woman of the past and the bicentennial rescue man, because that is pretty much the whole extent of what we get to know about these people during the first episode. Both of them are accompanied by an authoritarian sidekick figure who they can choose to either snub or obey in the game's few dialogue choices. Otherwise, the reason for their existence seems to be to feed us stuff to do.

Unfortunately, the stuff they're providing is very, very formulaic. Turn a valve. Flip a switch. Connect some wires -- Yes, I realize a janitor's regular day probably isn't that flashy in real life either, but come on! There's not an ounce of creativity at display here. The only thing missing is a hidden object scene.

I could maybe overlook the mundane puzzles if the gameplay was closer to Telltale's standards, but sadly that isn't the case. The camera angles have a tendency to mess up navigation since the viewpoint is usually switched when the character is already way too close to the screen border. However, a much bigger problem is the game's insistence on administering the clickable hotspots with a pipette.

Even if you can deduce a solution in advance, you usually have to try and fail or simply do the wrong thing first for the correct item to gain clickability. Did I mention that you also have to be reasonably close to a thing for it to show its icon in the first place? Well, you do.

I don't know. I'm all for new contenders entering the episodic adventure game space, but this here is not cutting it at all. With last years' Life is Strange, the bar originally set by Telltale has been raised; You cannot lower the standard well below the median and expect people to get hooked. During the final minutes of the first episode there's some very minor story intrigue, but nothing that'd compel me to buy the rest of the season. Nice facial animations, though.

I want to like this game. I really do.

After finishing two episodes however, I'm starting to see a pattern. There isn't any real gameplay in this "game". I was expecting a point & click adventure, something like Walking dead or Beneath a steel sky. Something where one would  collect items, and then combine them or use correct items at a certain spot. 

There is no such gameplay in the Descendant. You walk around with one single item, then use it in the very next room. No logic thinking required; The puzzles are no harder than using a blue keycard in the blue card reader. To make it even easier, those objects are the only ones that are available. If you manage to open a door in Doom, you'll manage everything this game throws at you.

On the plus side, the voice acting is acceptable. The story is decent enough that I'm looking forward to the next episode (sort of). I just hope that the episode will be less boring that the previous ones. Because I want to like this game. I really do.

I love Tell Tale type games such as Tales of the Borderlands and Wolf Among Us so when I heard about The Descendant I had to give it a go. The first episode is free which is something I wish more episodic games would do. The taster episode was enough to sell me on the rest of the season. It wasn’t the best of the genre but was solid and enjoyable. 

	The story was above average and kept me entertained. You play as a “janitor” in a post apocalyptic world. Janitors kept watch over cryogenically frozen people, coming out of cryo sleep themselves every so often, after a nuclear war wiped out most of the earth. You are tasked with waking up the “descendants” of ARK-01 two centuries after the war and a couple months after other ARKs have already woken. You will find though that your goals are not what you had first thought and that things didn’t go smoothly at this ARK. The game is a combination of choosing dialogue options that not only further the story and branch it as well as various puzzles. The puzzles range from annoying to easy but serve the purpose of breaking up portions of the game and giving you something different to do well. If the game didn’t have them I would probably be complaining how there wasn’t enough for me to do outside of dialogue. The choices themselves are fairly well done overall. They felt like they gave me a good portion of control over the story and allowed me to make it my own. The ending to the story was rather abrupt and could have used an extra cut scene or two to fill in the gaps at least to provide more of a hint about how things were after the end. I don’t mind having to use my imagination and not having things spelled out but this felt more vague than it should have been. The graphics overall are decent aside from the hair on the characters which was pretty poor. It was neither the best or worst I have seen from games using the Unity engine. 

	I played The Descendant on Linux using Valve’s Proton. It ran very well. I didn’t have to use any tweaks at all to get the game running. It didn’t crash on me at all. There was one scene where it only ran at 19 FPS but it only lasted for two minutes and then was back to normal. The game has a 30 FPS lock that is hard coded and can’t be changed. Luckily with a game like this it doesn’t hinder things too much as it isn’t a fast paced game and was at the full 30 FPS for the full game outside of that one scene with lag. There were a couple instances where there was some flickering on the floors but they only lasted a few seconds.  Alt-Tab worked without any issues. There were only two graphics options to adjust in the game. I played version 5.0 of the game from Steam. It took me about 6 hours to beat the game. My total system usage for RAM was between 3.3-3.7 GB of RAM while playing. It used between 19-25% of my CPU.

	I paid $3.39 CAD for the full season but can say it is easily worth the full price which is $16.99 CAD at the moment. At the very least give the free episode a try especially if you are a fan of the genre. It is a solid game overall which is enjoyable with a good story and gameplay.

I’ll give the dev team some credit, they did the best with what they have.  Is this a Telltale quality game? In my opinion, not at all. However, it falls in that category of experiences that remind me of watching a sci-fi tv show that is kinda mediocre, but for whatever reason I still keep watching it all the way to the end.  I say tv show and not movie, because if it were a movie I’d give up and move on.  The fact that it is in bite size chunks makes it more palatable. So, is it good?  In that regard, I feel it’s up to the player. From my personal point of view, it lies in that gray area of less than preferred but not wholly unacceptable.  It is potato chip quality, but that doesn’t make it entirely devoid of enjoyment.

For a quick synopsis, the world is ending and a select few are allowed to survive.  You get a bird's eye view of what it is like to be a “janitor” where you oversee the protection of the cryogenically preserved for the protection of the human race.  Somewhere in that dystopian predicament is the woven web of deceit that you must unravel. Any more detail is too spoily for my tastes.

What you should expect is a tale of a few twists with the occasionally angled and bent hook for the line and sinker of the drama. Whether that catches you is up to you, but I found it marginally enjoyable enough to see it to the end and, as I said, it feels a bit like an old sci-fi thriller short story that gets extended a bit.

The voice acting is adequate, and at times more than decent. I particularly felt like the Southern US accent for one of the characters felt extremely forced, but perhaps I’m not familiar with that exact part of the South.  In any case, the acting is adequate instead of the often stellar voice acting on a Telltale game, so know that going in.  This isn’t a Telltale Junior game or whatnot, it’s a half decent sci-fi tale that is acted with what the dev team could afford, and I think you should keep that in mind before plowing ahead.

If you are looking for puzzle gameplay, then look elsewhere.  The puzzles are very easy and only moderately challenging in the last sections of the game.  The focus here is on the story.  I thought there might be more emphasis on the actual choices, but I found they meant little even at the end of the game. Once I was finished, I didn’t feel much urge to replay.  So, keep that in mind, this is a one playthrough type of game.

With the main concentration of the game on the story, I felt it did a fairly adequate job of giving the player what they were after: a sci-fi story with a bit of a thrill.  That’s exactly what is provided, for better or for worse.  There are many sections that could have been expounded on, or clarified...but at the expense of making the game longer and more annoying, I think it’s brevity is perfectly fine.  For the $2 I paid for it, I’d say it was a decent purchase.  A short game with a somewhat interesting storyline, this is a good example of what you would expect for the price asked.  It’s quite hard to review a game that is almost entirely story driven without giving anything away. So, I suppose take this review with a grain of salt.  This game hits the microwave popcorn addled desire for something quick and moderately entertaining in lieu of the lack of Telltale games on the market. 6/10, not great but okay.

UPDATE: Some of my criticisms of the story were rendered moot by plot twists in later episodes, but this doesn't negate them being worthy of criticism IMO...just warranting a different form of criticism. Namely, that significant information about player characters is not known to the player early on, when it is relevant...which is just a cheat from a storytelling perspective.

There are some good ideas and intriguing plot details here, but some gameplay mechanic elements are immensely frustrating. This game makes me wish that Steam had a less binary review system, but as it is, I can't recommend this game.

For starters, one of the two playable characters is supposed to be a hand-picked expert who is responsible for the survival of a large portion of the remaining population of the human race, but the game treats the player assuming her role like a moron that needs to be handheld by dialogue catered to the lowest denominator. In spite of being one of only 4,000 people specifically selected to survive an apolocalype that wiped out the rest of humanity (you'd think the powers that be would be able to pick some competent people with that ratio), she has no idea what her job is or how to get around the facilty. The other "janitor" (term for the caretakers of the cryo bunker facilities) talks to her like she's an idiot, which turns out to be completely justified as almost all of the dialogue options available to the player make her seem like some random person who walked in off the street with no context of what is going on (the game tries to excuse this by her being a last minute rushed replacement, but it doesn't really work for a position so important). And the puzzles the player needs to complete as her are laughably simple in spite of her supposedly being some mechanical and/or engineering expert (there is a dialogue choice that even lets the player select what her specialty is, since it matters so little because nothing she does requires any technical knowledge).

The first crisis you must resolve as this character involves extremely simple puzzles, but also a lot of nonsense and logical problems that are disorientingly glaring. There is a problem. You look at the computer and it has the word "critical" clearly displayed. You go to solve the problem. Your partner gets on the radio and says "IT'S GONE CRITICAL!" Um...WHAT? It said that from the goddamn outset.

Then for some reason even though you are the one person tasked with rectifying technical problems in the facility, you have no idea of the basic layout of the facility and need to get directions, and there are keycode-locked doors that you were apparently never provided the codes for. Fortunately because this is a video game, those are just left lying around right beside the door (what the hell was even the point of that, from either a story or gameplay perspective?).

The storyline is divided between two characters, centuries apart, and the experience with the other character is equally illogical. You are performing a recovery/salvage mission and apparently brought NO TOOLS whatsoever, resulting in the need to pick up random tools off the ground along the way (how convenient that the right tool is always just lying around). The gameplay in that section is mind-numbing: you find one item after another and ALWAYS get messages along the lines of "its battery is missing," "it is out of fuel," "it is missing a part," etc, over and over and over and walk around finding the appropriate item three feet away to make the other item work.

But the frustrating gameplay mechanics are actually worse than the internal logic that leaves the player baffled by stupidity. You are given time-sensitve critical tasks and...

1.) You can't interact with objects during dialogue, and characters chat away like idiots.
2.) You run into scripted cutscenes that are unskippable and in which characters take far longer to realize something than a remotely intelligent player would.
3.) Movement is clunky at best. You left click to move and sometimes the character goes well away from where you want them to and you need to direct them to the right place repeatedly.
4.) Camera angles change jarringly and further complicate movement and cause misclicks.
5.) Characters don't act with any sense of urgency in respects that the player doesn't have control over (talking, taking forever to process things, inspecting things for excessive amounts of time and thinking through pointless commentary to themselves, dropping things, walking briskly instead of sprinting when they have seconds to spare to prevent people from dying, etc).
6.) If you click the wrong thing during a puzzle it usually delays you by several seconds while you hear your character say something along the lines of "that won't work." You can't interact with anything while this happens.
7.) You can't interact with objects unless you are positioned in the "right place," which is always guesswork and complicated by the bad movement and camera angles.
8.) You have to pointlessly stare at objects for several seconds after interacting with them before backing away from them, even after deducing they are useless.

The cumulative impact of all this clunky nonsense is that even though puzzle sections are not intellectually challenging whatsoever, 80% of the time you spend on them are wasted dealing with this frustrating BS (yes, I still completed the relevant sections within the alloted time limit, but it was not fun).

Oh also, you get achievements for everything. Including just starting the game. What an "achievement."

I like the basic story idea in broad strokes and there were moments that intrigued me (the computer selecting descendants to terminate at the end of the chapter was a highly that reinforced the "choices matter" gameplay), but it's unfortunately badly executed.

[h1]Episode 1 Review[/h1]
A lot of people are reviewing episode 1 and mentioning Fallout and TellTale games and I think that is a fair assessment. I, personally get strong vibes of Stanley Kubricks 2001: A Space Odyssey. It also reminds me of Zero Escape, a puzzle visual novel on 3DS and Vita. Anyways, on to the review.

[b]Length[/b]
Episode 1 is relatively short and introductory, it took me 50-55 minutes to complete, I felt I was relatively observant, I looked around each room, examined everything I thought I could before progressing so expect about that playtime for you, give or take 10 minutes. 

[b]Intro[/b]
You play as two characters, one from the past who is tasked with making sure that the survivors who were cryogenically frozen are all okay. These people are called janitors, they themselves get frozen as well and only wake up if there are issues. The other character you play is in the present, their job is to wake up all these sleeping survivors who for reasons unbeknownst to them, haven't woken up yet despite the surface being safe to live in again. 

[b]Controls & Gameplay[/b]
The controls are super easy, you click on where you want to move to and what you want to interact with. The only keyboard control I remember inputting was the 'E' button for certain basic QTE's. There are some relative basic puzzles featured but nothing that will have you scratching your head or maybe I've just been playing The Witness too much! Also at certain points you can choose what your character has to say, I'm not entirely sure how much influence these have on your playthrough yet but you see the typical "character x will remember that" text during certain decisions so I'm assuming we'll see the outcomes as we progress into later episodes. If you enjoy the gameplay approach of the TellTale games and Life is Strange then you'll also enjoy the game very much.

[b]Story[/b]
The story for me is where it shines, alongside the atmosphere. Even though it's very much an introduction, there are very subtle hints as to what is going on. For the first episode, it does all the right things, presents you with loads of questions as to what is going wrong and leaves you wanting for more. It's hard for me to talk too much about story without giving spoilers, especially as the first episode is relatively short, so I'll just say if you're familiar with and enjoyed the premise of  2001: A Space Odyssey, Fallout or Zero Escape then the story of this game will interest you.

[b] Constructive Criticism [/b]
If I were to criticise it for anything, I guess it would be the length of the first episode. It is a tad short, I'm hoping future episodes will be a bit longer. I think there were a few minor camera angle issues as well, but nothing that negatively affected the experience.

[b]Verdict[/b]
All in all, I'd recommend giving the game a try at the current price. It's hard to say how much your decisions influence the game at this point, but if the 'premise' at least has you interested. I find it very hard to believe after playing episode 1 you won't want to, no, need to play more. I hope these episodes arrive rather quickly!

Humanity has survived the apocalypse. A few centuries have passed and it’s now time to wake the survivors up and start anew. The game starts with two men gaining entry into ARK 01, the only bunker remaining which housed the descendants of mankind, with a simple task to wake up all these descendants from cryo sleep.

The story is split between the events of the present and those of the past and we are shown the developments of those almost in parallel to each other. The story takes place for the vast majority of its time within the ARK 01 bunker and follows a small handful of characters. It also follows a similar structure to Telltale Games, consisting of 5 episodes, each one about 1 - 1.5 hours long. 

Most of the gameplay is also quite similar to Telltale Games, being a simple point and click, with some puzzles, an odd quick time event, and timed dialogue choices. A lot of the time the puzzles were quite simple and involved mainly just finding an item to use on something. So, the gameplay is generally on the casual side. A few issues with character control and pathfinding came up, and at times the fixed camera angles were a tad annoying too.

Visuals and music are generally all right. Didn't particularly stand out to me, but were decent and serviced the game fine. The voice acting for each character is really good.

Overall, I was not exactly blown away by the game's story, and some of the events could've been executed with a bit more tension and build up, but it was quite a decent story in general and worth a playthrough once.

I'll file this game under casual gaming.  The presentation is more of a story driven narrative with some choose-your-own-adventure style cues.  The game does change depending on how you choose to handle some situations, but it seems that your choices still allow you to complete the game (I cannot confirm if speed to complete some puzzles has a negative impact as I did complete all in time).  

The puzzles are a mix of brain teasers, cryptography (low level) and some coordination type challenges.  Nothing is incredibly complicated, but many are quite fun.  My only issue with the puzzles is that they don't really seem to fit into the story line.  For example (spoiler): [spoiler]In one puzzle, you upgrade your security clearence by connecting a number of dots in sequence through a maze.  I guess it is supposed to represent hacking, but it falls short.[/spoiler]

Controls in the game are easy enough to follow.  I would recommend playing with a controller because it seems to make movements a little easier.  But there are a lot of automatic camera angle changes of several degrees or even opposite angles where your controls are suddenly off kilter; you may be traveling right when camera changes and suddenly your traveling left.  This will lead to many occasions where you'll cycle between to camera angles, which can get frustrating.

The storyline is pretty solid and surprisingly less predictable than I thought.  I was drawn in quite well by how the story unfolded.  The voice acting was pretty decent throughout the game (it's not the best of Hollywood, but it can hold its own and it's believable).  

Replayability:  Admittedly, the storyline doesn't have enough variation to warrant replay.  I went back to get a few of the achievements, but it was too tedious to go through everything again.  But let's be honest: There aren't many storyline driven games that are interesting enough to draw me back in for multiple play-throughs.

All-in-all, it's a good game.  It may not be for everyone, but it is appealing to those who love story-driven games.  It was a good casual game that I could play without bending my brain too much.  But don't get the game expecting loads of action or seriously challenging puzzles...because it's not like that.

But trust me, you're not playing this for the puzzles or the gameplay. You're playing this for the expertly presented drama and the "Oh shit!" moments set in a great looking science fiction environment.

Overall, there's not a whole lot here, but what is here is absolutely worth the asking price. $2.99 for 1 hour seems fair to me.

Sometimes I was quite surprised. 

The graphics are a bit older and not the best, but that doesn't matter at all in this game. 
Nevertheless, the science fiction apocalyptic setting is extremely well designed with great attention to detail.

The voice acting and sound are great. 

The controls are point and click. Sometimes it's confusing when the camera angle changes.

And, of course, you have to make decisions during the dialogues that affect the rest of the game – sometimes you only have a limited amount of time to decide. 

I bought the game for €1.49, which was a really good bargain. It was definitely worth it and I was really well entertained overall. 

There are also negative points that really need to be considered.

Firstly, after completing the game for the first time, there is no option to skip the dialogues and cutscenes on the second playthrough.

This game is similar to the Telltale games in the same way water is similar to vodka. It has the same vibe but where the TT games are a series of escalating horrible events with agonizing decisions to be made about which flavour of bad you want, the Descendant is definitely closer to a point and click, with fewer decisions and more puzzle elements, held together by a casually unravelling narrative. It has the usual annoyances that come with the Unity engine but I didn't experience any major bugs or crashes in my playthrough. The voice acting is pretty decent. One of the technicians near the end sounded a little dicey, but the strong performances for Donnie and Randolph really helped immerse me. Most importantly, the story is good, well written and paced well. It managed to hold my interest the whole way. At full price, it's an ok game, if a little short. However, at its discounted price, the shortness works in its favour and it;s practically a must buy. If it were much longer it feels like it might run out of steam and only limp to the finish line. As it is, you get a night or two of entertainment with a punch at the end. Ultimately, if you're itching for an experience that has that Telltale vibe, pick it up during the sale and you'll likely enjoy it a lot. If the devs make another game like this I'd like to see them shift one way or the other, either drop the telltale "X will remember that" entirely and focus on the story and puzzles or actually have more of those decisions and make them matter. Either way, here's hoping there will be more.

[b]TL;DR: The Descendant is a fantastic episodic game exploring human nature, desperation and the feeling of wanting to fight for what you believe in. While a little clunky and rough around the edges, the charm of the game and the well written story drives you forward in this ~6 hour adventure.[/b]


Episodic games have become all the rage these days; Telltale and Dontnod have been pioneering this style of game, and Gaming Corps contributes to it with The Descendant. All episodes are rather short and can usually be completed within 60 to 90 minutes, which in my opinion is a great length for a game like this.

This game takes place on an apocalyptic earth. After missiles have struck our planet, humanity has fled into so called Arks, underground bunkers overseen by the "Janitors". These janitors are responsible for making sure these arks run smoothly. Once their time comes, the remnants of humanity, the descendants, are supposed to wake up from their cryosleep and populate the world yet again. But things obviously don't go quite so smoothly...

You play a variety of characters in different stages of the game. The game controls in a point´n click manner - click on the ground, walk there. The movement is a bit clunky sometimes, as are the animations, but it ain't terrible. You can interact with some objects, pick them up and use them to solve puzzles. The puzzles in this game, and there will be quite a few, range from very easy to slightly difficult, but they are never unsolvable. As is the usual case in these games, you also have to make plenty of decisions, some of which have an influence on the story. Unlike some other episodic games, however, most of the decisions are somewhat superficial and only a few influence how the story progresses and ends; but having the choice is always neat.

The story of the game is, as it should be, the main draw. It is well written, entertaining and interesting enough to make you want to see the end. The voice acting is the real kicker - the voices range from good to, well, "interesting". Especially Donnie, one of the two main characters, reads his lines with such zeal that you can't help but feel excited with him. Seriously, the voice acting is very charming - it isn't always "good" (though it never drifts down into bad territory), but it always has some sort of charm to it that is hard to describe.

The game can be completed in about 6 hours, which is an ideal time to bond with the characters, to love or hate them, and to see your decisions affect the story. While the movement can be a bit clunky and the voice acting a bit odd, the game has an inexplicable charm to it - the kind of charm where you realize that a lot of effort and, especially, [b]love[/b] went into the creation of it. It's definitely worth playing and I don't regret any cent spent - I'd even recommend it at full price.

Personal rating: 8.5/10.
